**Supplementary Figure 1\. Individual participant data from Experiment 1 before pooling across test colors. (a)** Proportion of downward responses for the red test stimuli. **(b)** Proportion of upward responses for the green test stimuli. These responses were pooled across test colors (for details, see **Figure 2**) to obtain the psychometric functions shown in **Supplementary Figure 2**.

**Color-separated analysis (Experiment 1).** The main text pools responses across the two test colors (see **Figure 2**). Fitting the psychometric functions separately for each color (panels **a** and **b** above) and comparing the misbinding and control conditions within each color, using the same Bayesian paired t-test as the main analysis, found moderate evidence for a PSE shift for red test stimuli alone (BF₁₀ = 6.37), whereas green test stimuli alone showed no such shift (BF₁₀ = 0.43); a direct comparison of the red and green PSE differences found only anecdotal evidence that the two colors differed from one another (BF₁₀ = 2.15). Because the color–motion pairing was fixed rather than counterbalanced across participants (see Methods), this color-specific pattern could reflect either a genuine misbinding-induced bias specific to the color–motion pairing used here, or an unrelated color-specific response bias unconnected to misbinding; the present design cannot distinguish these possibilities. The pooled null result reported in the main text remains the primary, preregistered outcome measure. Slope estimates showed no comparable color-specific pattern (red BF₁₀ = 0.31, green BF₁₀ = 0.34; color-symmetry BF₁₀ = 0.33, moderate evidence that the two colors did not differ).

**Supplementary Table 1\. Prior-sensitivity and design-sensitivity analyses.** *Prior-sensitivity*: each paired Bayesian t-test reported in the main text (PSE and slope, excluded and all-participant samples, Experiments 1 and 2) was recomputed under four Cauchy prior widths (rscale): narrow (r = 0.2), medium (r = 1/√2, the default reported in the main text), wide (r = 1), and ultrawide (r = √2). BF₁₀ values are shown for each; qualitative conclusions (evidence for H0 vs. inconclusive vs. evidence for H1) were unchanged across prior widths for every comparison except the Experiment 2 slope comparison, which remained in the anecdotal-for-H1 band (BF₁₀ 1.5–1.8) across all four widths and never reached the moderate-evidence threshold (BF₁₀ \> 3) under any tested prior.

*Design-sensitivity analysis*: for a true paired Cohen's *d* of 0.2, 0.5, or 0.8, we simulated 2,000 replications of a paired Bayesian t-test (default medium prior) at each of the sample sizes retained in this study (n = 7, 10, 12) and recorded the proportion of simulated replications reaching BF₁₀ \> 3 (evidence for H1), BF₁₀ \< 1/3 (evidence for H0), or an inconclusive result in between.

**Supplementary Method: Hierarchical logistic mixed-effects model.** The main text's Bayesian and frequentist comparisons (**Figures 3, 4**) use a two-stage approach: a four-parameter logistic psychometric function is fitted to each participant's trial-level responses separately (quickpsy; Linares & López-Moliner, 2016), and the resulting per-participant PSE and slope estimates are then submitted to paired comparisons between conditions. This approach treats each participant's point estimate as equally reliable and provides no principled way for a noisy or poorly behaved individual fit to contribute partial information; participants whose fits were judged unreliable were instead excluded outright (see Methods). As a robustness check on this two-stage approach, we additionally fitted a single hierarchical (trial-level) logistic mixed-effects model directly to the raw, un-aggregated binary responses of all participants, using partial pooling to let each participant's estimate be informed by, and shrunk toward, the population-level estimate, without requiring any participant to be hard-excluded.

For each experiment, we fit the binomial mixed-effects model `opposite_to_ind_response ~ sospeed * nowblocktype + (sospeed * nowblocktype | Subnum)` using the `glmer` function of the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) in R, with a logit link function. `opposite_to_ind_response` is the trial-level binary response (1 = judged the test stimulus as moving in the direction opposite to the inducer, 0 = otherwise); `sospeed` is the signed test speed relative to the inducer's motion direction; and `nowblocktype` is the adaptation condition (misbinding vs. control, with control coded as the reference level). The fixed-effect coefficient for `nowblocktype` is therefore analogous to the condition-related shift in the intercept of the psychometric function evaluated at `sospeed` = 0 — a trial-level analog of the PSE-shift comparison in the main analysis — while the `sospeed:nowblocktype` interaction coefficient is analogous to the condition-related change in the slope of the psychometric function, a trial-level analog of the slope-difference comparison. The random-effects term `(sospeed * nowblocktype | Subnum)` allows each participant's intercept and both slopes to vary around the population-level estimate, with the covariance structure among the random effects estimated from the data (a maximal random-effects specification given the fixed-effects structure). Models were fit with the bobyqa optimizer (`glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))`) to improve convergence given the complexity of the random-effects structure relative to the sample size.

This model does not include lapse or guessing-rate parameters, because a standard binomial GLMM has no upper or lower asymptote free to depart from 0 and 1; it is therefore not a full trial-level replacement for the quickpsy-based analysis (which fixes these rates at 0.03; see Methods), but a partial-pooling robustness check on whether the two-stage PSE-shift and slope-difference conclusions depend on that specific two-stage, exclusion-based analysis strategy. Some fitted models returned a singular-fit warning, indicating that at least one random-effects variance or covariance component was estimated at a boundary value (typically zero); this is a common outcome for a near-maximal random-effects structure fit to a sample of this size and should be borne in mind when interpreting the precision, though not necessarily the point estimates, of the coefficients reported in **Supplementary Table 2**. For each experiment, the model was fit twice: once to the excluded sample used in the main analysis, and once to all twelve participants without exclusion, mirroring the two samples reported for the two-stage analyses in the main text.

Code: `Perception_manuscript/revision/hierarchical_glmm_check.R`.

**Supplementary Table 2\. Supplementary hierarchical (trial-level) logistic mixed-model check.** Added in response to the suggestion that a hierarchical trial-level psychometric model would be more appropriate than fitting each participant's psychometric function independently and then submitting the point estimates to a paired t-test (the two-stage approach used for the main analyses). We fit `opposite_to_ind_response ~ sospeed * nowblocktype + (sospeed * nowblocktype | Subnum)` as a binomial mixed-effects model (`lme4::glmer`; Bates et al., 2015) to the raw trial-level responses, with participant-level random intercepts and slopes partially pooled toward the population estimate, so that no participant needed to be hard-excluded. This model does not include a lapse/guess parameter and is therefore a partial-pooling robustness check on the PSE-shift and slope-difference conclusions, not a full replacement for a trial-level Bayesian model with an estimated lapse rate; some models returned a singular-fit warning (a variance component estimated at the boundary), which is common with this sample size and random-effects structure and should be borne in mind when interpreting the precision of the estimates below.

| Experiment | Sample | Term | Estimate (logit) | SE | *z* | *p* | 95% CI |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | ----: | ----: | ----: | ----: | :---- |
| Exp 1 | excluded, n=10 | Condition (PSE-shift analog) | 0.102 | 0.145 | 0.70 | .482 | \[–0.18, 0.39\] |
| Exp 1 | excluded, n=10 | Speed × Condition (slope-diff analog) | –0.071 | 0.356 | –0.20 | .843 | \[–0.77, 0.63\] |
| Exp 1 | all, n=12 | Condition (PSE-shift analog) | 0.071 | 0.119 | 0.60 | .550 | \[–0.16, 0.31\] |
| Exp 1 | all, n=12 | Speed × Condition (slope-diff analog) | –0.020 | 0.279 | –0.07 | .943 | \[–0.57, 0.53\] |
| Exp 2 | excluded, n=7 | Condition (PSE-shift analog) | 0.012 | 0.070 | 0.17 | .866 | \[–0.13, 0.15\] |
| Exp 2 | excluded, n=7 | Speed × Condition (slope-diff analog) | –2.866 | 0.782 | –3.66 | **\< .001** | \[–4.40, –1.33\] |
| Exp 2 | all, n=12 | Condition (PSE-shift analog) | –0.020 | 0.071 | –0.28 | .781 | \[–0.16, 0.12\] |
| Exp 2 | all, n=12 | Speed × Condition (slope-diff analog) | –1.576 | 0.745 | –2.12 | **.034** | \[–3.04, –0.12\] |

For Experiment 1, neither term approached significance in either sample. For Experiment 2, the PSE term was similarly nonsignificant, whereas the slope-difference term reached significance in both samples (excluded sample: *p* < .001; all participants: *p* = .034).
